newsitem.title: USA: Perry, Christopher seek end to Latam arms ban.
newsitem.headline: Perry, Christopher seek end to Latam arms ban.

text.p: The outgoing U.S. secretaries of state and defence have urged President Bill Clinton to end a virtual ban on high tech arms sales to Latin America, U.S. officials said on Wednesday.

Such a policy shift, proposed in a memo to the White House by departing Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Defence Secretary William Perry, could open a potential lucrative market to the limping U.S. defence industry.

"They did sign a memo and send it to the White House within the past few weeks," Navy Cmdr. Joe March, a Defence Department spokesman, told Reuters in response to questions. "The subject was the consideration of arms sales to Latin America on a case-by-case basis."
Christopher has in the past publicly opposed such an easing of the ban because he believed it might fuel an arms race in the region.

But other U.S. officials said privately on Wednesday that the secretary of state had been persuaded by Perry that the time had come for change because all Latin American nations except Cuba were now democracies.
Clinton is expected to visit Latin America early this year, perhaps in March, and a new policy replacing a decades-old ban could be in place by then, the officials said.

Retiring Republican Sen. William Cohen of Maine, nominated by Clinton to replace Perry, earlier signed a letter with 39 other senators urging the White House to ease the policy on a case-by-case basis.
Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright's position on the issue is not known.

Cohen and Albright are expected to take office within weeks, and could quickly send signals to the White House, where officials of the National Security Council are currently considering the Christopher-Perry memo, officials said.

Argentina has voiced fears publicly that opening the door to such sales could spark an arms race in the region. But Perry told Latin American defence ministers at a meeting there in October that countries in the region should be allowed to modernise their militaries.
Argentina is in the process of buying 36 older A-4 "Skyhawk" U.S. fighter jets, but Brazil, Chile and perhaps other countries are planning to modernise their air forces with even more advanced jets.
Peru last year bought a squadron of MiG-29 fighter jets, among the world's most advanced warplanes, from Russia.
Perry told reporters in Bariloche, Argentina, in October that disputes over borders and other tensions among Latin American nations were on the wane and that democracy was now the order of the day.

"Now we have 34 democratic nations and border disputes are becoming a thing of the past," he said. "Because of that fundamental change in circumstance, we believe it is appropriate to re-examine policy."
